text:
Recent work distinguishes similarity from complementarity rather than treating both as generic relatedness. Allegro’s [Suggest, Complement, Inspire (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03702) adapts text-based two-tower retrieval to separate recommendation intents; [LLM-Enhanced Reranking (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16237) studies reranking specifically for products used together. These support separate diagnostic hypotheses: substitute, complement, and duplicate. They do not establish that co-purchase proves compatibility or that textual similarity proves a redundant purchase.

Practical synthesis for the available data: extract prerequisite and compatibility statements from titles/descriptions, retaining the supporting text and item identifiers. Distinguish explicit contradiction, explicit support, and insufficient evidence. A stated device-model restriction can support a conflict when history identifies a conflicting model; an absent prerequisite purchase cannot establish non-ownership. Normalize titles, model numbers, editions, and bundle contents to flag potential duplication, while treating replenishment and alternate editions as unresolved. These are proposed diagnostics, not validated conclusions from the cited recommendation studies.

Abstention also needs evaluation. [AbstentionBench (2025)](https://github.com/facebookresearch/AbstentionBench) tests underspecified and unanswerable cases and reports persistent weaknesses across models. For this task, abstain from unsupported rejection explanations while preserving recommendation ranking. Report evidence coverage and unknown rates alongside contradiction and duplicate flags; validate ranking changes using macro validation HR@10. Any available explicit user feedback should remain distinct from inferred reasons. Histories alone cannot establish rejection motives, current ownership, or unobserved diversity/conformity traits.
